title: Daily midpoint extremes align less often than maximum extremes across eight US coast pairs in 1996-2024
abstract: We compared same-date high-water extremes across six US tide gauges in 1996-2024. We used 61,199 daily records from 30 NOAA source objects. We removed monthly mean sea level from daily maxima and from daily midpoints. Each measure used its own site and calendar-month 95th percentile on the same valid dates. Across eight Atlantic-Pacific pairs, the mean joint-day rate was 0.984% for maxima and 0.198% for midpoints. The difference was 0.786 percentage points, with a paired three-year block interval of 0.619 to 0.974 points under fixed thresholds. A later check that refitted thresholds gave an interval of 0.703 to 0.867 points. Maximum extremes exceeded a within-block year-pairing reference at all 15 site pairs after correction for 30 tests. Midpoint extremes did so at five pairs, all on the same coast. The daily midpoint removes half the observed daily range from the maximum by definition. It is not a storm-surge measure. These results limit the use of maximum-date alignment as evidence of shared weather. They do not prove a tide mechanism or independent weather between coasts.

display.caption: Left: joint extreme-day rates on the same eligible dates, with separate 95th percentiles. Right: paired three-year block intervals for maximum minus midpoint concurrence. Intervals use fixed fitted thresholds. Opposite-coast pairs form the primary group. Other groups are descriptive.

citations.reason: We build on the published cross-coast maximum alignment result, its site set, and its timing reference. We prepare our own paired maximum and minimum evidence from the shared raw snapshots.
The published two-Atlantic-site midpoint test informs the measure and its limits. We extend the comparison to all six sites and a different period and timing reference.
